354.history: The mill on the bend of the river is the heart of the coal country. Six sacks of its hill's coal went down to the strangers in the first years, and the first contract was read aloud at the mill. Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill took A' Chompanaidh's staff here and a house with a slate roof, and his son Dòmhnall, his grandson Iain and his great-granddaughter Mòrag held it after him, until Mòrag broke it across her knee on the Company's step in the hundred and forty-eighth year. Seven men drowned in its flooded gallery, and the inquiry struck her testimony out. On the twenty-eighth of an Gearran in the hundred and forty-ninth year its people took the walled store at first light, and the war began here. Its mill still ground grain for the central country through all the years of the coal, and the steelyard ledgers of its weigh-house, in which the hill's coal had been set down by the ton since the first contract, burned green in the ledger fires of the hundred and fiftieth year.
354.known_for: the overseer's staff, and the first morning of the war

280.history: The wild hill in the middle country gave its name to the Eleven of Cnoc fhiadhaich, the crew of the first great fall, whose orphans went to Cill thais. Raghnall asked three times for timber at the heading before the roof came down. The road around Doire mhòr was cut through its ground, and the Company's huts followed. The wall of its old heading still stood above the camp at the close of the age, and the crews would not work the gallery beneath it.

109.history: The large village on damp ground beside the sacred wood of Macha took in the orphans of the Eleven of Cnoc fhiadhaich, in a long house of stone with new thatch that its custodians made ready at the end of the street, and raised them. The wood behind it gave shelter in the last years to the priests who had left the capital's temple, and the forest council of the war sat among its fires. The long house the custodians made ready stood at the end of the street for the rest of the age, and the orphans raised there were counted in its roll as children of the town.

383.history: The low ford below the new workings became the first of A' Chompanaidh's camps: timber huts where the ferrymen had always put the carts across in the wet season, and a Company store where the clerk had no book for cheese. The families who came down from Doire mhòr and the hill villages went to its huts, and the spotted pox and the fever were worst among them. Its roll was the one in which the line of Aisling was first found. The ford floods every wet season and the ferrymen still put the carts across, and the camp grew into a town of rows beside the old crossing. Its chaplain in the spotted pox wrote every dead man, woman and child in a fair hand.

313.history: The old river port in the hollow of the rock was made a coal landing early in the age, and its barge-stage took the hill's coal down the Abhainn uaine for more than a century. In the first winter of the war a Company ship came up the river and shelled the stage to keep it from the rebels; three-and-twenty of the fishing town behind it died, and the ship burned island coal to do it. Its walls follow Macha. The Leaden Hawk passed the burned stage on the first day of their walk north and found a woman sorting stone from ash with her bare hands at what had been her hearth.
313.known_for: the shelling of the coal stage

224.history: The camp town of the deep workings was laid out on the Company's paper before a stone of it was cut, in straight rows, the first town of the Dia-thìrich drawn by a surveyor. Two of its streets came down in the year of the edict of seizure for a spoil-tip, and the families took huts at Àth ìseal or went to kin in the hill villages. Most of its hewers came from the camps at Àth ìseal and Achadh dhomhain, and the grid of its streets was the pattern for every camp the Company drew after it.
